text:
# Cell projection

Also called: Projected Polyhedra, Projected Tetrahedra (when restricted to tetrahedral meshes), Cell-based volume rendering

## Overview
Cell projection is a [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) technique that treats volumetric data as a set of geometric primitives (cells), projects them onto the 2D image plane, and rasterizes the resulting polygons using hardware-accelerated or software-based scan-conversion [S1][S4, book][S2][S3, unofficial]. It solves the performance bottleneck of sequential [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) by leveraging the efficiency of rasterization pipelines, while differing from particle-based methods (like [splatting](#23-splatting.md)) by maintaining explicit geometric boundaries [S1][S2]. Unlike [object-order ray casting](#6204-object-order-ray-casting.md), it strictly separates the projection/scan-conversion phase from the global composition phase to reduce asynchronous communication overhead in parallel implementations [S4, book].

## Shared principles
The cell projection family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric primitives that are transformed and rasterized [S1][S3, unofficial][S4, book].

1.  **Primitive Representation:** The volume is decomposed into primitives. These may be explicit geometric shapes (cubes, cells, splats) or implicit functions sampled via texture hardware [S1][S3, unofficial][S4, book].
2.  **Transformation:** Primitives are transformed from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or specific factorizations (e.g., [shear-warp](#24-shear-warp.md)) [S2][S3, unofficial][S4, book].
3.  **Rasterization:** The transformed primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane. This step leverages hardware-accelerated scan-conversion, depth testing, and blending [S1, S2][S3, unofficial][S4, book].
4.  **[Compositing](#2436-compositing.md):** Contributions are accumulated to form the final image. This is typically done using [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md) in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly [S1, S2][S3, S7, unofficial].
5.  **Hardware [Acceleration](#18-acceleration.md):** Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity [S1, S2][S3, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Parallel Cell Projection](875-parallel-cell-projection.md)
[Parallel Cell Projection](#875-parallel-cell-projection.md) is a distributed-memory and shared-memory strategy for volume rendering that decomposes the volume into geometric primitives (cells), projects them into screen space, and rasterizes them using hardware-accelerated or software-based scan-conversion. It solves the performance bottleneck of sequential cell projection by parallelizing the computationally expensive polygon generation and the subsequent image-space composition. Unlike object-order ray casting, it leverages the efficiency of rasterization pipelines, while differing from concurrent scan-conversion/composition methods by strictly separating the projection/scan-conversion phase from the global composition phase to reduce asynchronous communication overhead.

### [Cell Projection with Texture Mapping for Opacity](993-cell-projection-with-texture-mapping-for-opacity.md)
This method accelerates the cell projection rendering technique by using hardware texture mapping to compute the exponential transparency term $\exp(-\int \tau ds)$ per pixel via table lookup. It solves the problem of visual artifacts known as Mach bands, which arise when the integrated opacity $\alpha$ is linearly interpolated across projected polygons. By interpolating the linear parameters $\kappa_{avg}$ and $l$ in hardware and using a 2D texture lookup for the exponential, the method avoids per-pixel exponential calculations while maintaining visual correctness. It builds on [Cell projection](26-cell-projection.md).

### [Topological Sort for Cell Projection](999-topological-sort-for-cell-projection.md)
[Topological Sort for Cell Projection](#999-topological-sort-for-cell-projection.md), commonly known as [Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering (MPVO)](#845-mpvo-meshed-polyhedra-visibility-ordering.md), is an object-space algorithm that computes a correct back-to-front visibility ordering for volume rendering on convex meshes composed of convex polyhedral cells. It solves the problem of determining the rendering order required for correct alpha compositing by constructing a directed adjacency graph based on local face-sharing relationships and performing a topological sort. It sets itself apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives by relying exclusively on the mesh topology and convexity to guarantee correctness in $O(n)$ time, avoiding the expensive geometric ray-shooting queries of [XMPVO](1363-xmpvo.md) or the image-space rasterization of [SXMPVO](944-exact-visibility-ordering-for-cell-projection-volume-renderi.md). Unlike [Convex Grid Topological Visibility Sorting](2370-convex-grid-topological-visibility-sorting.md), which is a specific application of this principle, MPVO is the general algorithmic framework described by Williams and Max.

### [Parallelized Accurate Sorting for Projected Tetrahedra](1128-parallelized-accurate-sorting-for-projected-tetrahedra.md)
[Parallelized Accurate Sorting for Projected Tetrahedra](#1128-parallelized-accurate-sorting-for-projected-tetrahedra.md) is a view-dependent sorting algorithm designed to resolve the parallelization bottlenecks inherent in standard [projected tetrahedra](#877-projected-tetrahedra.md) rendering. It solves the dependency and sequence limitations of neighboring tetrahedra by employing logical partitioning to enable parallel processing. Unlike standard topological sorting which is constrained by global dependencies, this method divides the dataset into spatial blocks along the viewing direction, allowing for the parallel peeling of unobstructed layers. It sets itself apart from its siblings by introducing a specific four-step pipeline that combines spatial blocking with logical boundary partitioning to maintain accuracy while enhancing parallelism.

### [GPU-based Cell Projection for Structured Data](1864-gpu-based-cell-projection-for-structured-data.md)
This method is an interactive volume rendering technique for large, regular (structured) volumetric data sets on GPUs. It solves the performance bottleneck of general Projected Tetrahedra (PT) by eliminating redundant projection and visibility sorting computations through the exploitation of data regularity and orthographic projection. Unlike general PT, which requires expensive cell sorting, this method achieves constant-time traversal order and reuses projection parameters for all voxels, dedicating over 60% of processing time to the rendering pipeline itself. It consumes less memory than Hardware-Based Ray Casting (HARC) while achieving high rendering speeds.

### [Cell Projection with Scan-line Conversion](1968-cell-projection-with-scan-line-conversion.md)
[Cell Projection with Scan-line Conversion](#1968-cell-projection-with-scan-line-conversion.md) is a software-based direct volume rendering method that rasterizes volumetric primitives (such as tetrahedra or hexahedra) using scan-line algorithms to leverage spatial coherence, avoiding the need for expensive graphics hardware acceleration. It solves the problem of rendering irregular and multiple grids efficiently by decomposing primitives into triangles and accumulating color and opacity front-to-back along scan lines. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as [Parallel Cell Projection](875-parallel-cell-projection.md) which focuses on hardware parallelization, and [Cell Projection with Texture Mapping for Opacity](993-cell-projection-with-texture-mapping-for-opacity.md) which uses texture hardware, by relying entirely on software scan-line coherence to produce image quality equivalent to ray casting but with fewer artifacts than hardware [Gouraud shading](#4645-gouraud-shading.md).

### [Cell-Projection Rendering](4279-cell-projection-rendering.md)
[Cell-projection rendering](#4279-cell-projection-rendering.md) is a parallel volume rendering technique for unstructured data that projects mesh cells into image space, generating ray segments that are merged in image space. Unlike ray-casting, it does not require pre-sorting cells in depth order, offering greater flexibility in data distribution and higher accuracy than slice- or vertex-projected methods. It builds on [Cell projection](26-cell-projection.md) by utilizing hardware-accelerated scan-conversion of geometric primitives.

### [Tetrahedral representation and traversal](4396-tetrahedral-representation-and-traversal.md)
This family renders volumetric data by decomposing the volume into [tetrahedral primitives](#1389-tetrahedral-strips-and-fans.md), projecting them onto the 2D image plane, and rasterizing them to accumulate color and opacity. It solves the problem of rendering unstructured or irregular grids with high performance by leveraging hardware-accelerated rasterization instead of [ray marching](#6739-ray-marching.md). Unlike [Tetrahedral Volume Rendering](820-tetrahedral-volume-rendering.md) which often relies on GPGPU techniques to compute projection geometry and intersection parameters in a first pass, [Projected Tetrahedra](877-projected-tetrahedra.md) uses explicit geometric projection and scan-conversion.

### [3D Cube Projection and Rasterization](6678-3d-cube-projection-and-rasterization.md)
[3D Cube Projection and Rasterization](#6678-3d-cube-projection-and-rasterization.md) is a software rendering technique that transforms the geometric faces of a 3D [voxel cube](#4076-voxel-data-layout.md) into 2D screen space and draws them as filled polygons. It solves the problem of visualizing individual volumetric cells by treating them as explicit opaque or semi-opaque quads rather than sampling them via raycasting or texture mapping. It differs from hardware-accelerated rasterization by performing all matrix multiplications, perspective division, and pixel writing in software, and from standard raycasting by relying on explicit polygonal face projection and depth culling rather than per-pixel ray traversal.

### [Sorting-free Pre-integrated Projected Tetrahedra](7491-sorting-free-pre-integrated-projected-tetrahedra.md)
[Sorting-free Pre-integrated Projected Tetrahedra](#7491-sorting-free-pre-integrated-projected-tetrahedra.md) ([PBVR](#4247-particle-based-volume-rendering-pbvr.md)) is a volume rendering technique for irregular datasets that eliminates the need for explicit visibility sorting of tetrahedral cells. It solves the scalability issues of conventional sorting-based methods and the low image quality (visible footprints) of particle-based methods by treating volume rendering as a stochastic process. Unlike its sibling [Parallel Cell Projection](875-parallel-cell-projection.md) which may require sorting, PBVR controls fragment rendering probability based on opacity, allowing semi-transparent compositing without alpha-blending or back-to-front ordering.

### [Incoherent Projection](7541-incoherent-projection.md)
[Incoherent projection](#7541-incoherent-projection.md) is a cell-based volume rendering method that renders the 2D projection of general convex hexahedra by decomposing each cell's silhouette into an arrangement of planar polygons. It solves the problem of handling the high number of nondegenerate projection topologies inherent in irregular hexahedral grids, where the projection shape varies significantly between cells and viewpoints. Unlike coherent projection methods that assume uniform topology across the volume, incoherent projection analyzes each cell individually in screen space, making it robust for curvilinear grids but computationally more expensive.

### Screen Space Area Calculation
Calculates the projected area of a tetrahedron in normalized screen space to determine refinement criteria or culling. Uses cross products to compute wedge areas, which are twice the triangle area, then divides by four [S5, unofficial]. Project tetrahedron vertices $T, L, R, B$ to screen space using camera projection: $T \leftarrow \text{camera.projectPoint}(T)$, $L \leftarrow \text{camera.projectPoint}(L)$, $R \leftarrow \text{camera.projectPoint}(R)$, $B \leftarrow \text{camera.projectPoint}(B)$. Calculate area sum using cross products of vertex vectors: $\text{area} \leftarrow |(L-T)\times(R-T)|+|(R-T)\times(B-T)|$. Add remaining terms: $\text{area} \leftarrow \text{area}+|(B-T)\times(L-T)|+|(L-B)\times(R-B)|$. Return final area divided by 4: $\text{return area} / 4$. Triangles cover the total area twice in projection, and cross products yield wedge areas (twice triangle area), necessitating division by 4 [S5, unofficial].

### Pre-integrated classification for cell projection
A method to determine color and opacity contribution by applying pre-integrated classification, using scalar values on front and back faces and thickness as texture coordinates for a 3D texture map storing volume ray integral values [S6]. Parameters include $s_f$ (scalar value on the front face), $s_b$ (scalar value on the back face), and $l$ (thickness resulting from scan converting the tetrahedron) [S6].

### CellFast
A software algorithm for interactive unstructured volume rendering that moves computations for order-independent transparency and volume scan conversion from [CPU](#10688-naive-sdf-generation-cpu.md) to graphics hardware, eliminating the need for a software sorting pass [S7, unofficial]. The algorithm follows these steps: I. Preprocess dataset. For a new viewpoint: II. Visibility sort cells. For every cell in sorted back-to-front order: III. Test plane equations to determine class (1,2,3,4). IV. Project and split cell unique frontback faces. V. Compute color and opacity for thick vertex. VI. (Hardware) Scanconvert new triangles. In the original CellFast implementation on OpenGL accelerated desktops, Steps II-V (visibility sorting, plane equation testing, projection/splitting, and color/opacity computation) saturate the host CPU, leaving the graphics hardware running below capacity [S7, unofficial]. In experiments with CellFast, an average of 3.4 triangles are written per tetrahedron during the splitting process [S7, unofficial].

## Background
Cell projection was developed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory by Peter Williams, Claudio Silva, Richard Cook, and Peter Max [S1, S2]. It is one of the four main paradigms of volume rendering, alongside raycasting, splatting, and shear-warp [S3, unofficial]. The method was designed to handle curvilinear and unstructured grids directly, avoiding the need for resampling [S1][S4, book]. It addresses the challenge of non-planar faces in curvilinear grids by subdividing "problem cells" into tetrahedra with planar faces [S4, book]. The technique has been parallelized for distributed-memory and shared-memory systems to handle large datasets [S1, S2][S4, book].
